passage:
Hi Sumit bhaiya,
Remember you told me I'd never sit for homework without Ma shouting? Well. I found a trick. There's one playlist, the old film songs you put on my phone before you left for Bengaluru, and I only let myself hear it while doing homework. Not on the bus, not before sleeping. So now at five o'clock I actually want to open my books, because that's when the songs come. It works great for geography maps and copying notes. But yesterday I tried it with the maths chapter on proofs and got nothing done: I kept singing along and lost the steps. So proofs are silent now, songs after. Ma says she can't believe it. Write back soon?
Mridul

qa.q: When does Mridul let the playlist play?
qa.a: Only while doing homework, not on the bus or before sleeping.

qa.q: Why does Mridul now want to open the books at five o'clock?
qa.a: Because five o'clock is when the favourite songs come; the saved pleasure turns starting into a small treat instead of a fight.

qa.q: What choice did Mridul make after the proofs went badly?
qa.a: To keep proofs silent and play the songs afterward, since singing along pulled attention away from the steps.

qa.q: How might Ma see the change?
qa.a: Ma, who used to shout to get homework started, is surprised and relieved that Mridul now sits down without a battle.

grounding: A teenager reserves a favourite playlist for homework, which eases starting, but finds proofs need silence.

passage: Hi everyone, I'm Kashish from Class 11, and the radio club asked me to talk about how I stopped dreading homework. So. I have this one playlist, soft covers of old ghazals, that I love more than almost anything. Last year I made a rule: I only get to hear it when my books are open. My brother Sachin thought I was mad. "Just listen to it whenever, na?" But it changed things. At seven, when I'd normally stall, I think about those songs and I sit down. Starting stopped hurting. The one thing I learned the hard way was essays. I tried writing my English essay with the playlist on and everything came out rhythmic and meaningless. For essays and new chapters, I need silence. The songs are for practice sums.

qa.q: What playlist does Kashish save for homework?
qa.a: Soft covers of old ghazals.

qa.q: Why does thinking about the songs help Kashish sit down at seven?
qa.a: The songs are something Kashish loves and only gets with the books open, so the wish to hear them outweighs the urge to stall.

qa.q: Which choice about essays shows good judgement?
qa.a: Keeping essays and new chapters silent after noticing the music made the writing rhythmic but meaningless, and saving the playlist for practice sums.

qa.q: Why might Sachin have found the rule strange at first?
qa.a: To Sachin a favourite playlist is something to enjoy any time, so rationing it seems pointless until the change in Kashish's homework shows its purpose.

grounding: A teenager saves a loved playlist for homework to make starting easier, and learns that some tasks need silence.

passage: I'm Kashish, and I spent the summer holidays at my cousin Sachin's flat in Lucknow. Every afternoon at four he'd put on the same headphones, the big blue ones, and open his chemistry workbook. Nobody else was allowed to touch those headphones. One day I borrowed them to hear what was so special: a playlist of cricket commentary remixes, which he'd told his mother he listened to "only for homework". I teased him. He shrugged and said it was the only reason he sat down at all. And he did sit, every day, for an hour. But when his board practice paper came, he took the headphones off, put them in the drawer and wrote in total silence. I never asked why. Maybe the paper needed all of him.

qa.q: What did Sachin do with the headphones when the board practice paper came?
qa.a: He took the headphones off, put them in the drawer and wrote in total silence.

qa.q: What does Sachin's shrug and reply suggest about how he feels about homework?
qa.a: Starting homework seems hard for him, and the playlist is the pleasure that gets him to the desk at all; the shrug suggests he isn't embarrassed to need it.

qa.q: Which choice of Sachin's shows he knows the limits of the trick?
qa.a: Putting the headphones away for the practice paper, since a timed paper needs the full attention that the music would split.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Sachin's headphone rule?
qa.a: As a visitor Kashish finds it funny and teases him, but notices he really does study every day, and can only guess why he goes silent for the paper.

grounding: A cousin observes a teenager who keeps a playlist for homework only and drops it for work that needs full attention.

passage:
Sunday: Kiran, fifteen, sat down to do homework and got up four times: water, snack, messages, water again. Nothing got done. Kiran's older sister Salma said, "Try what I did in college. Pick music you love and play it only when you study."
Tuesday: Kiran chose the old qawwali playlist and kept it away from every other part of the day. At five, headphones on, the first song started and Kiran was already opening the geography workbook. Maps, labels, colouring, done in forty minutes.
Friday: Maths test revision. Kiran put the playlist on but kept reading the same word problem three times, humming along. Finally the headphones came off. "This one needs quiet," Kiran told Salma. "Music's for maps."

qa.q: Which playlist did Kiran choose?
qa.a: Kiran chose the old qawwali playlist.

qa.q: What does Kiran's quick start on Tuesday suggest about how the playlist felt?
qa.a: The playlist felt like a treat Kiran had been missing, so sitting down to homework felt less like a chore and more like getting the music back.

qa.q: What choice did Kiran make on Friday, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Taking the headphones off for maths; the word problems needed full attention, so Kiran saved the music for easier tasks like maps.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing 'Music's for maps'?
qa.a: Salma may be pleased the tip worked and that Kiran adapted it instead of copying it blindly, noticing which tasks need silence 😊

grounding: A teenager saves a favourite playlist for homework, which makes starting easier, but finds that maths needs silence.

passage: Tanvir, I see those earphones go in every time the chemistry book comes out. Let me tell you about me at fourteen, in Lucknow, long before phones. I'm your Sudha Nani, and back then our house had one radio. On Wednesday evenings it played old film songs for an hour, and I adored them. My mother made a deal: the radio was mine on Wednesdays only if my homework sat open in front of me. Suddenly I raced to the table at seven. Essays, map work, copying notes, all done humming. But algebra, never. When I tried algebra with the songs, I'd look up at the end and find the page still blank. So algebra got the quiet corner on Thursday mornings. Music helps you start. Not every task wants company.

qa.q: When did the radio play old film songs?
qa.a: On Wednesday evenings, for an hour.

qa.q: Why did young Sudha suddenly race to the table at seven?
qa.a: She adored the songs and could only have the radio with her homework open, so sitting down felt like a reward instead of a chore.

qa.q: What did Sudha do when algebra didn't work with the songs, and how could Tanvir use that?
qa.a: She moved algebra to a quiet corner on Thursday mornings; Tanvir could keep the earphones for easier work and give hard chemistry problems silence.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see those earphones differently after the story?
qa.a: Tanvir might see them as a treat worth saving for homework, while asking honestly whether the chemistry needs the music or just quiet.

grounding: A grandmother recalls reserving a favourite radio hour for homework as a teenager, which helped her start, while algebra still needed silence.
